# I. INTRODUCTION
**I** NTERNET of Things (IoT) real-time monitoring devices based on climate change are considered a new technology in many important sectors, such as food security. The impact of climate change (i.e., floods, droughts, extreme temperature, and wildfire) on food security and livelihoods is widely acknowledged [[1]](#page-8-0). The effects of climate change on food security and livelihoods are viewed on various perspectives through studies on climate change impacts, vulnerabilities, and adaptation (IVA) [[1]](#page-8-0). Thus, monitoring the food quality, controlling food that approaches its shelf life, and enhancing inventory management and store layout are necessary. IoT application, for instance, can help the actors reduce food loss and waste to support food supply chain systems. Simultaneously, the sensor technology can reduce food loss and waste to support food supply chain systems by managing the ideal physical environment, particularly in terms of temperature and humidity [[2]](#page-8-1).
The sensor can be utilized over the entire product's shelf life and supply chains (production, storage, distribution, and consumption). Sensing sensors installed on industrial equipment could be used to gather data on raw material consumption during the production stage, including that of water, electricity, and other inputs [[3]](#page-8-2). Food temperature and air humidity measurements can also be obtained from sensors in warehouses during the storage phase [[4]](#page-8-3). Sensors aboard vehicles can measure the distance traveled, the weight of the goods being transported, and the amount of fuel used during the transportation phase [[4]](#page-8-3). Any level of the supply chains could yield environmental emission data using intelligent sensors and environmental monitoring systems [[3]](#page-8-2), with implications in accuracy, traceability, transparency, and controllability. IoT is expanding rapidly and has the potential to be
a huge information source. Although these new technologies are expected to lead to more sustainable and effective food chains in the coming years, their potential applications in the food field are limited. In recent years, however, their potential in the food industry has drawn remarkable attention. These monitoring devices are used to monitor food delivered as humanitarian aid to people in areas affected by natural disasters, and they are expected to improve the sustainability of food chains by reducing food loss and waste [[5]](#page-8-4).
According to [[6]](#page-8-5), numerous IoT real-time monitoring devices were presented and discussed on the basis of the various points of sustainable sensing parameter. Despite the existence of these monitoring devices, no superior monitoring device addresses all sustainable sensing parameters simultaneously. In addition, all researchers considered these points in the development of IoT real-time monitoring devices. However, no research has assessed and modeled the identified IoT real-time monitoring devices to determine which is the most and least sustainable based on the sensing parameters. Three assessment concerns must be addressed to fill this research gap. First, multiple sustainable sensing parameters (attributes) must be considered [[7]](#page-8-6), [[8]](#page-8-7), [[9]](#page-8-8). Second, these attributes must be prioritized on the basis of their importance level [[10]](#page-8-9), [[11]](#page-8-10), [[12]](#page-8-11). Third, variance in data is another concern that must be considered when assessing and modeling IoT real-time monitoring devices [[13]](#page-8-12), [[14]](#page-8-13), [[15]](#page-8-14). Consequently, determining the most and least sustainable IoT real-time monitoring devices and the value of the remaining parameters may change depending on how one parameter is changed, resulting in a complex multiattribute decision-making (MADM) problem [[16]](#page-8-15), [[17]](#page-8-16), [[18]](#page-8-17), [[19]](#page-8-18). Various MADM approaches for selecting the optimal alternative amongst a list of alternatives have been developed by scholars [[11]](#page-8-10), [[20]](#page-8-19), [[21]](#page-8-20). The MADM approach is required to bridge the research gap and tackle the problem's complexity.
The contributions of this study can be summed up as follows: 1) formulating a decision matrix (DM) by intersecting IoT real-time monitoring devices with sustainable sensing parameter attributes; 2) a new extension of fuzzy-weighted zero-inconsistency (FWZIC), called fuzzy weighted with zero inconsistency method and circular intuitionistic fuzzy sets (C-IFS-FWZIC), is formulated and developed for weighting sustainable sensing parameter attributes involved in modeling IoT real-time monitoring devices; and 3) a new integrated MADM between C-IFS-FWZIC and additive ratio assessment (ARAS) based on a formulated DM as a decisioning methodology is developed to model IoT real-time monitoring devices and identify the optimum sustainable ones.
The remainder of this article is structured as follows. The most related works are examined and discussed in Section [II.](#page-1-0) Section [III](#page-2-0) presented in depth the DM development, design of the C-IFS-FWZIC method, and integration of ARAS with the developed C-IFS-FWZIC method. IoT real-time monitoring devices for minimizing food loss and waste to support food supply chain systems during and after natural disasters are reported in Section [IV](#page-4-0) along with the decision matrix, attribute weights, and uncertain modeling findings that were obtained. In Section [V,](#page-6-0) the proposed MADM approaches' robustness
is assessed and validated. The conclusions are presented in Section [VI.](#page-8-21)
# II. THEORETICAL MADM JUSTIFICATION
MADM is a subfield of operations research that includes various approaches and applications in different fields [[22]](#page-8-22). In the literature, many MADM modeling approaches, such as a simple additive weighting method (SAW), weighted product model (WPM), and ARAS [[23]](#page-8-23), have been utilized. However, ARAS aids the formation of rational decisions depending on the utility level of each alternative. Utility is a function value that, when applied to the best alternative, generates a rather sophisticated efficiency value, which affects the significance and worth of the attributes [[24]](#page-8-24). The strengths of ARAS depend on in its ability to: 1) comprehensibly perform computations; 2) identify notions that are logical and straightforward; and 3) prioritize weights that are determined by comparisons. Therefore, it has been confirmed to be effective in addressing numerous MADM problems [[25]](#page-8-25), [[26]](#page-8-26).
However, ARAS has one major limitation, that is, its inability to prioritize the set of attributes based on their relative importance [[27]](#page-9-0). Many researchers have combined the AHP weighting method to cover this limitation on ARAS [[28]](#page-9-1), [[29]](#page-9-2). The primary deficiency of the AHP method is the inconsistency caused by pairwise comparisons. In 2023, Qahtan et al. [[30]](#page-9-3) addressed the problem of inconsistency by proposing a new MADM weighting method named the FWZIC. Since then, it has been utilized extensively to determine the weight of the assessment attributes without inconsistency. In addition, FWZIC requires neither a large number of mathematical operations nor a huge amount of time to operate. In general, the different weighted attributes in FWZIC are independent; thus, adding or eliminating them does not entail a recalculation. Moreover, gathering feedback from decision-makers (DMs) in FWZIC is straightforward, and the initial version was extended under a triangular fuzzy set (FS), which cannot appropriately manage the vagueness and uncertainty of information [[31]](#page-9-4).
To address these issues [[32]](#page-9-5), the FWZIC method was created using interval-valued spherical and hesitant two-tuple, probabilistic-hesitant, Fermatean, Pythagorean m-polar, dualhesitant, neutrosophic, spherical [[28]](#page-9-1), and T-spherical [[19]](#page-8-18) FSs, as well as linear Diophantine fuzzy rough sets. Notwithstanding these attempts, informational ambiguity and uncertainty continue to be some open issues [[30]](#page-9-3), [[31]](#page-9-4), [[32]](#page-9-5).
Zadeh [[33]](#page-9-6) developed the notion of FS to address the ambiguous information by creating type-2 FSs to allow membership functions to include the fuzziness of membership degrees as a third dimension. Instead of introducing uncertainty to the membership function, the overall goal of other FS extensions' is to consider the DMs level of reluctance. The goal of the recently established FS extension known as circular intuitionistic FSs (C-IFSs) is to provide fuzziness to membership functions, as it does in type-2 FSs [[34]](#page-9-7). An MADM method that can fuzzify the membership function as in type-2 FSs and account for DMs hesitation, such as in intuitionistic FSs, is required in [[34]](#page-9-7).

The concept of reluctance to FSs was initially introduced in intuitionistic FSs. The most recent development of FSs is the circular IFS, created by [[35]](#page-9-8) in 2020. Contrary to IFSs, a C-IFS represents each element using a circle with the coordinates A(x), A(x), and radius *r*. These sets are those in which each element of the universe has a degree of membership and a degree of nonmembership, and a circle around them has a radius *r* such that the sum of the degrees of membership and nonmembership within this circle is at most equal to 1. C-IFSs can be used in MADM approaches to consider the properties highlighted [[34]](#page-9-7).
To our knowledge, no prior studies have extended FWZIC under C-IFS. More so, the integration of C-IFS-FWZIC and ARAS methods has not been applied to any case study. Thus, we are motivated to propose novel C-IFS-FWZIC and ARAS to model IoT real-time monitoring devices and identify the optimum sustainable ones, which considered the main objectives of this study. The C-IFS-FWZIC is formulated and developed to calculate the weight of sustainable sensing parameter attributes. The ARAS method is used to model IoT real-time monitoring devices using the derived weights. Minimizing loss and waste of supply chain systems is crucial during natural disasters.

## *B. C-IFS–FWZIC Method Development*
Uncertainties and inaccuracies can be effectively addressed by integrating the FWZIC method into the C-IFS environment. The following steps outline the formulation of the C-IFS-FWZIC method.
*Step 1:* At this stage, the predefined sustainable sensing parameter attributes are explored to assess and model the IoT real-time monitoring devices.
*Step 2:* At least three DMs with prior experience in IoT real-time monitoring devices are identified and selected to construct a structured expert judgment (SEJ). In addition, an assessment form is designed and endorsed by the DMs in this step. The preferences on the attributes of the DMs are represented by five linguistic scales, as shown in Table [II,](#page-2-3) and gathered using the designed form.
*Step 3:* The sustainable sensing parameter attributes for the IoT real-time monitoring device alternatives are crossed with the three preselected DMs to construct the expert decision matrix (EDM), as shown in [(1).](#page-3-0) For further analysis, linguistic terms gathered by the assessment form in the preceding step are replaced with a numerical scale in Table [II](#page-2-3)
$$ EDM = \begin{bmatrix} E_{11} & \cdots & E_{1m} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ E_{n_E 1} & \cdots & E_{n_E m} \end{bmatrix} (1) $$
where n_E is the number of experts and m is the number of attributes
Step 4: IFS-EDM is created by applying the numeric scale with the IFS numbers (IFSNs) listed in Table II on the EDM, to obtain IFS-EDM having the following form:
$$ \widetilde{\text{EDM}} = \begin{bmatrix} (\alpha_{11}, \beta_{11}) & \cdots & (\alpha_{1n_A}, \beta_{1m}) \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ (\alpha_{n_E1}, \beta_{n_E1}) & \cdots & (\alpha_{n_Em}, \beta_{n_Em}) \end{bmatrix}. \tag{2} $$
In the following steps, the C-IFS is used to determine the radius which unveils uncertainty .... The C-IFS and C-IFSN are defined as follows.
Definition 1 [34]: E is assumed a fixed universe. A C-IFS S_r in E is an object with the following form:
$$ S_r = \{ \langle x, \mu_S(x), \nu_S(x); r \rangle | x \in E \} $$
where 0 \le \mu_S(x) + \nu_S(x) \le 1.
S_r is known as Circular-IFS, r \in [0, 1] is the radius of the circle around every element x \in E, and the functions \mu_S:E \to [0, 1], and \nu_S:E \to [0, 1] indicates the degree of membership and level of nonmembership for the element x to the set S_r through E. The formula for calculating the degree of uncertainty (indeterminacy) is as follows:
$$ \pi_S(x) = 1 - \mu_S(x) - \nu_S(x). \tag{3} $$
A circle with center (\mu_S(x), \nu_S(x)), and radius r is used to symbolize each element in C-IFSs. Let c_1 and c_2 be two circular intuitionistic fuzzy numbers represented by c_1 = < \mu_{c_1}(x), \ \nu_{c_1}(x); \ r_1 > \text{and} \ c_2 = < \mu_{c_2}(x), \ \nu_{c_2}(x); \ r_2 >. They produce outcomes with a minimum and maximum levels of uncertainty. Thus, the operations presented here are based on the minimum and maximum of the radiuses independently. The definition of how they operate is shown in [34].
Step 5: For C_j = \{(\alpha_{ij}, \beta_{ij}) | i = 1, ..., n_E\} an IFS, calculate the arithmetic average of the IFNs using the following equation:
$$ \langle \overline{\alpha}(C_j), \ \overline{\beta}(C_j) \rangle = \left( \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_E} \alpha_{ij}}{n_E}, \ \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n_E} \beta_{ij}}{n_E} \right). \tag{4} $$
Step 6: The radius lengths produced by DM when evaluating the *j*th sustainable sensing parameter attributes are considered to determine the maximum radius lengths. The maximum radius length R = (r_j)_{1 \le j \le m} based on the decision matrix of DM is obtained using
$$ r_{j} = \max_{1 \le i \le n_{E}} \sqrt{\left(\overline{\alpha}(C_{j}) - \alpha_{ij}\right)^{2} + \left(\overline{\beta}(C_{j}) - \beta_{ij}\right)^{2}}. (5) $$
Step 7: The circular intuitionistic fuzzy attribute weight matrix, (\langle \mu_j, \nu_j; r_j \rangle)_{1 \leq j \leq m} is obtained using the DM made of intuitionistic fuzzy pairs \widetilde{\text{EDM}}, defined in (2), by applying the intuitionistic fuzzy weighted averaging (IFWA) operator shown in (6) [36]
$$ \begin{alignat*}{2}(1) && \text{IFWA} (A_1, \ldots, A_n) &= \sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{1}{n} A_j \\ \text{of} && &= \left(1 - \prod_{j=1}^{n} (1 - \alpha_{A_j})^{\frac{1}{n}}, \prod_{j=1}^{n} \beta_{A_j}^{\frac{1}{n}}\right) \quad (6)\end{alignat*} $$
where A_j = (\alpha_{A_j}, \beta_{A_j}) are IFNs. Indeed, (\mu_j, \nu_j) = IFWA ((\alpha_{1j}, \beta_{1j}), \ldots, (\alpha_{n_Ej}, \beta_{n_Ej})) for j = 1, \ldots, m.
Step 8: Equations (7) and (8) are used to calculate the optimistic attribute weight matrix Q^o = (q_j^o)_{j=1,\dots,m} and the pessimistic attribute weight matrix Q^p = (q_j^p)_{j=1,\dots,m}, respectively. The circular intuitionistic fuzzy attribute weight matrix is transformed into the intuitionistic fuzzy attribute weight matrix, using the membership functions and radius. Here, two distinct attribute weight matrices, namely, the optimistic attribute weight matrix, are produced depending on the decision maker's attitude toward optimism and pessimism
$$ Q^{o} = \begin{bmatrix} (\mu_{1} + r_{1}, \nu_{1} - r_{1}) \\ (\mu_{2} + r_{2}, \nu_{2} - r_{2}) \\ \vdots \\ (\mu_{n_{A}} + r_{n_{A}}, \nu_{n_{A}} - r_{n_{A}}) \end{bmatrix} \tag{7} $$
where q_i^o = (\mu_i + r_i, \nu_i - r_i).
$$ Q^{p} = \begin{bmatrix} (\mu_{1} - r_{1}, \nu_{1} + r_{1}) \\ (\mu_{2} - r_{2}, \nu_{2} + r_{2}) \\ \vdots \\ (\mu_{n_{A}} - r_{n_{A}}, \nu_{n_{A}} + r_{n_{A}}) \end{bmatrix} \tag{8} $$
where q_i^p = (\mu_j - r_j, \nu_j + r_j).
Step 9: The score function provided in (9) is used to calculate optimistic and pessimistic attributes' scores
$$ Score((\alpha, \beta)) = \alpha - \beta \tag{9} $$
for any IFN (\alpha, \beta). Indeed, the scores are calculated as follows:
$$ s_j^o = \operatorname{Score}(q_j^o) and s_j^p = \operatorname{Score}(q_j^p). $$
Then, optimistic and pessimistic attributes' scores weights obtained by scaling the scores as follows:
$$ w_j^o = \frac{s_j^o}{\sum_{j=1}^m s_j^o} \text{ and } w_j^p = \frac{s_j^p}{\sum_{j=1}^m s_j^p}. (10) $$
Step 10: Each attribute's combined weight is calculated by applying the following formula [37]:
$$ w_{j} = \frac{c + w_{j}^{o} \times w_{j}^{p}}{\sum_{j=1}^{m} (c + w_{j}^{o} \times w_{j}^{p})} (11) $$
for j = 1, 2, ..., m, and c > 0 is a predefined number to guarantee positive weights.

## C. ARAS Method Adaptation
In this section, the resulting sustainable sensing parameter attributes (Section III-B) are fed to ARAS [22] to model the IoT real-time monitoring devices and determine the most and least sustainable model directly proportional to the utility function value, thereby defining the complex relative efficiency of a feasible alternative, as shown in the following steps [22].
Step 1: The decision-making matrix (DMM) is formed during this step. The following DMM of preferences from nfeasible alternatives (rows) rated on m attributes (columns) is used in the MADM of the discrete optimization issue to represent any problem that needs to be solved
$$ X = \begin{bmatrix} x_{11} & x_{12} & \dots & x_{1m} \\ x_{21} & x_{22} & \dots & x_{2m} \\ \vdots & \vdots & \vdots & \vdots \\ x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \dots & x_{nm} \end{bmatrix} \tag{12} $$
where m is the number of alternatives, n is the number of attributes that describe each alternative, x_{ij} is a value that represents how well the ith alternative performs in relation to the jth attribute, and x_{0i} is the best value for the attribute j. If the j attribute's optimal value is unknown, then
$$ x_{0j} = \max_{i=1}^{n} x_{ij}, if \max_{i=1}^{n} x_{ij} is preferable (13) $$
$$ x_{0j} = \max_{i=1,\dots,n} x_{ij}, \text{ if } \max_{i=1,\dots,n} x_{ij} \text{ is preferable} x_{0j} = \max_{i=1,\dots,n} x_{ij}, \text{ if } \max_{i=1,\dots,n} x_{ij} \text{ is preferable.} (13) $$
Step 2: All attributes' initial values are normalized, defining the values \bar{x}_{ii} of the normalized DMM \bar{X}.
1) The attribute's maximum preferred values are normalized as follows:
$$ \bar{x}_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij}}{\sum_{i=0}^{n} x_{ij}}. (15) $$
2) The attribute whose preferable values are minimum is normalized using a two-stage procedure
$$ x_{ij}^* = \frac{1}{x_{ij}}; \ \bar{x}_{ij} = \frac{x_{ij}^*}{\sum_{i=0}^n x_{ii}^*}. (16) $$
In this stage, a normalized weighted matrix is defined. It is to be noted that the optimal solutions x_{0j} are involved in the normalization process.
Step 3: The weights' coefficients obtained from C-IFS-FWZIC (w_i)_{i=1,\ldots,m}, defined in (11), are used
$$ \sum_{j=1}^{m} w_j = 1. $$
Step 4: The following formula is used to calculate the normalized weighted matrix:
$$ \widehat{x}_{ij} = w_j \overline{x}_{ij} for i = 0, \dots, n and j = 1, \dots, m (17) $$
where w_i denotes attribute's weight (importance), and \bar{x}_{ij} is the normalized rating of the j attribute.
Step 5: The next stage is finding the values of the optimality function
$$ S_i = \sum_{i=1}^{m} \widehat{x}_{ij}, \text{ for } i = 0, \dots, n. (18) $$
S_i represents the optimality function value for alternative i. The IoT real-time monitoring device alternatives are ranked according to the optimality function values, the higher the value the better is the alternative.
Step 6: The degree of alternative utility is ascertained by contrasting the variant under analysis with the ideal best one S_0. The following equation is used to determine an alternative utility degree K_i:
$$ K_i = \frac{S_i}{S_0}; for i = 0, ..., n (19) $$
where S_i and S_0 are the values of the optimality attribute, determined by (18).
Evidently, the calculated values K_i are in the range [0,1] and can be arranged in the desired order of precedence, an increasing sequence. The values of the utility function indicate a complicated relative efficiency of the practicable alternative [22]. Algorithm 2 in the supplemental file presents the pseudocode of the ARAS Method.
# IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
## A. Decision Matrix and Procedure of Evaluation Results
The DM was constructed by intersecting the lists of the IoT real-time monitoring devices and their sustainable sensing parameter attributes. Table A.I in the supplemental file presents the attributes within the proposed DM that is used to model IoT real-time monitoring devices. The results for the procedure of evaluation attributes, as described in [5] evaluated 54 IoT real-time monitoring devices based on the presence or absence of ten sustainable sensing parameter attributes. The presence or absence of each sustainable sensing parameter attribute was recorded as "Yes" or "No," and these values were converted into binary values of "1" and "0" for the purpose of this research. This matrix illustrates the score values that are assigned to each evaluated IoT real-time monitoring device based on the predefined attributes. The sustainable sensing parameter attributes are binary in nature (i.e., 1/0), where "1" indicates that the sustainable sensing parameter attributes were considered during the IoT real-time monitoring device design, and "0" indicates that sustainable sensing parameter attributes were ignored during the IoT real-time monitoring device design. The constructed matrix is fed to ARAS with C-IFRS-FWZIC to model the IoT real-time monitoring devices. The following section reports the weighting findings and the sustainable sensing parameter attributes derived using the C-IFRS-FWZIC method.

# VI. CONCLUSION
Using the implications of this work, researchers and developers of sustainable IoT real-time monitoring devices-based climate change to minimize food lose and waste of food supply chains systems during natural disasters. The food supply chains sector can also gain significantly from choosing the best sustainable IoT real-time monitoring devices. The suggested work does, however, have three primary limitations. First off, the three hired experts were not modeled in order of experience. Using only five linguistic expressions and numerical scales, the EDM was created. Third, the IC-IFS-FWZIC method was limited to the IFWA operator and S(A) score function. Future research may concentrate on: 1) determining the experts according to their expertise to produce more accurate results; 2) investigating seven or ten linguistic expressions and a numerical scale to formulate the EDM; 3) utilizing additional operators with the C-IFS-FWZIC method to aggregate and defuzzify values; and 4) employing yet another FS.
